name: Zero-Based Budgeting
title: Zero-Based Budgeting
answer: Zero-based budgeting is a planning method in which every cost must be justified from a zero base for each new budget cycle, rather than being carried forward from the prior period. In forecasting and planning, it sits alongside incremental budgeting and driver-based planning, and it is used most often for operating expenses, discretionary spend, and shared services. The work depends on granular cost data, clear ownership of decision units, and a repeatable way to rank competing requests. Artificial intelligence enters mainly as a way to classify spend, surface patterns, and test scenarios at a scale that manual review cannot match.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practice runs on the same financial data foundations as other planning work, including general ledgers, enterprise resource planning systems, cost center hierarchies, and cloud data warehouses. Teams often use spreadsheets for local models and dedicated planning platforms for consolidation, version control, and workflow. AI components may include classification models that map transactions to cost drivers, anomaly detection that flags unusual spend, and natural language interfaces that let planners query budget packages. The quality of the output depends on clean master data, consistent account mappings, and reliable vendor and contract records.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins by defining decision units, which are the smallest areas of spend that a manager can control and justify. Teams then map cost drivers, build zero-based packages for each unit, and rank those packages against strategic priorities and funding limits. AI can assist by clustering similar spend, detecting outliers, generating first drafts of cost narratives, and running sensitivity analyses across many scenarios. Human reviewers still decide what to fund, because the method is as much about governance and trade-offs as it is about calculation. The result is a budget that shows what each activity costs and what would be lost if it were removed.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance for zero-based budgeting covers data rights, provenance, audit trails, and the controls that keep cost allocations defensible. Every figure traces back to a source system, a contract, or an approved assumption, and any AI-generated classification or narrative needs a review path. This atlas tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, which reflects how closely budgeting controls sit to audit, reporting, and internal policy. Model risk also matters, because biased or opaque cost drivers can disadvantage some units and hide real obligations. In practice, teams document model versions, training data, and the human approvals that turn a draft package into a committed plan.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Zero-based budgeting is moving from a periodic exercise toward a more continuous planning capability, supported by better data pipelines and faster scenario tools. AI is likely to take on more of the routine classification, variance explanation, and package drafting, while humans focus on prioritization and trade-offs. The method is also converging with driver-based forecasting, rolling forecasts, and cost transparency initiatives that ask for the same granular data. As planning cycles shorten, the main constraint is less about computation and more about trust in the numbers and the governance around them.
